newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK -- 3-year Treasury note auction.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK -- 3-year Treasury note auction.

text.p: The first of the Treasury's $39.75 billion three-part quarterly refinancing auctions -- the $17.75 billion three-year Treasury note auction -- should be the fulcrum for U.S. government securities trading on Tuesday, analysts said.

As it did on Monday, range-trading will likely prevail before Tuesday's three-year note auction. The question for players is whether foreign participation in this auction will be more subdued after a G7 meeting this weekend seemed to alter the dollar's prospects in the foreign exchange markets.

The G7 nations meeting in Berlin signaled their desire to curb the dollar's ascendance against other major currencies. The dollar weakened on the G7 statements, but then reversed itself as dollar bulls focused on the fundamental strength of the U.S. economy versus those of its major trading partners.

James Griffin, Jr., senior vice president and investment strategist at Aeltus Investment Management, Inc. which manages $37.0 billion in assets, said the bonds should take the Treasury refunding in stride, but said the new emphasis on two-way risk in the foreign exchange markets could soften Japanese demand for the new U.S. securities.
But Chris Rupkey, vice president and financial economist at Bank of Tokyo/Mitsubishi, said he thought foreign demand at the Treasury three-year note auction would remain unaltered.

"Generally, when they buy, it's for reasons of yield differentials," said Rupkey. "And more importantly, overnight (interest) rates are so low in Japan that demand will not change because of what the G7 has said.

"No one looks for the dollar to weaken substantially against the yen," said Rupkey. "They're just looking for it to stabilize. Dollar strength has been building for two years and it's not going to come to a screaching halt."

Before the 1300 EST/1800 GMT bidding deadline for the three-year note auction, the market gets several economic reports, none influential enough to push the market out of its current current range. The BTM/Schroders weekly chain and department store sales report is due at 0900 EST/1400 GMT. The January survey of area business conditions from the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond is due an hour later. In December, the survey's shipments index read -2. Its service sector index read five. Forecasts for the current month were not available.
The only government data -- on fourth quarter productivity and unit labor costs -- are also due at 1000 EST/1500 GMT.

Productivity and unit labor costs, forecast to be up 2.1 percent and 1.4 percent, respectively, generally do not move the market, economists said, but they might arouse interest this time, given the market's concern about the potential inflationary impact of hourly wage gains.

"Fourth-quarter productivity and labor costs might get some attention because it could help the market on the inflation story," said Elliott Platt, managing director of economic research at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette. Platt's forecast is for 2.5 percent Q4 productivity growth and 1.5 percent labor cost growth."

"Typically, (quarterly) productivity is not a big market mover but this report should show a rather large increase in productivity and a good reading on unit labor costs, so the market might take some notice of that," said Daiwa Securities America Inc chief economist Michael Moran, who sees a three percent productivity gain and a 0.5 pct unit labor cost rise.
The 6-1/2-percent benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury bond was quoted down 2/32 to 97-11/32, yielding 6.71 percent in late trade on Monday.
Dealers indicated that Fed funds would open at 5-3/16 percent on Tuesday. (( -- 212-859-1679 ))
